thread_title: Helonias bullata West Virginia Swamp Pink
breadcrumb: Helonias bullata West Virginia Swamp Pink

posts.body_html:
Also known as the swamp pink, Helonias bullata is a rare and threatened plant that has a beautiful pink inflorescence. It also reportedly has a pungent, spicy fragrance! In the wild, the plants flower during February thru April-ish, although flowering time greatly depends on the weather and temperature. Interestingly, you'll often see plants in full bloom having really ragged looking leaves: this is because the previous season's leaves last quite a while! When it freezes or gets damaged by rain/full sun, the leaves get messed up easily! During the peak of their bloom, the current season's new leaves are just emerging!

The plants require a winter dormancy and emerge from an underground rhizome, which can be divided to make more plants. It is still poorly understood what triggers flowering, but most likely it's due to reaching a certain vegetative maturity, having good growth momentum the previous year, being healthy during that whole time, experiencing a decrease in photoperiod during the fall and experiencing a proper winter dormancy period.

Helonias bullata is typically found growing in part to full shade: during the winter, a lot of the trees that otherwise shade the plants will lose their leaves and give the plants more direct sunlight. As spring arrives, the trees cause deeper shading. Sphagnum is commonly seen growing alongside this plant, indicating they require nutrient poor, acidic soils. Because of their propensity to self pollinate, this species is vulnerable to inbreeding depression. The seeds mature relatively quickly and are reportedly only viable for a short period of time. They can float on water, which allows them to be dispersed downstream, thereby helping the species proliferate in new environments.

As of 2024, these are super challenging to acquire in the US, but the genetics have have fallen into some motivated hands, so that will change hopefully in the near future.

Much like Sarracenia, the species is threatened because of habitat loss, habitat alternation, unscrupulous collecting, and of course the elephant in the room, climate change which is like habitat loss. Like carnivorous plants, they appear to grow in nutrient poor soils and prefers to have the soil fully hydrated at all times. They are often times found growing right on the side of springs and in boggy areas.

As I learn more about this species, I'll post updates but what I can say so far is that out of what appeared to be many hundreds of seeds, only a few of them sprouted! They didn't require any stratification, and I have them growing fully protected indoors under lights since their rate of survival with slugs, pill bugs, birds, and all the enemies of Mike Wang that live outside is pretty low otherwise.

So far, they seem to be growing relatively fast! These seedlings are almost 3 months old and for comparison, the sarracenia seedlings that germinated at the same time are about 3X smaller! They were sown directly on 100% peat, were not buried as the seeds require light to germinate, and only given reverse osmosis water so far. I haven't fed them yet but they probably need a weak application of maxsea 1-2X a months, the leaves are starting to look a little chlorotic.... they will get fed soon! Pics taken 3/18/24:







To be continued....

posts.body_html:
Hey! Cool to see someone else trying to grow this plant. I picked up a plant a couple years ago and through it in my outdoor bog here in Ohio. right on about the blooming part of it. It bloomed the first year after i got it, but haven't seen much since. I was able to divide it once though so I have a backup.
Hopefully I can treat it better this summer with some more sunlight and get a bloom next year.

Thanks for sharing!

posts.body_html:
Ok, totally unexpected but one of these plants actually pushed out a flower! What triggers them to bloom? No clue, I for sure am still very new to this plant and don't have it fully figured out yet. The great news is that several of the plants are producing side shoots, which means I should be able to divide them and get them into circulation in the near future. How do you divide them? Oh man, that's going to be tricky to figure out, I'm guessing you have to do that during the winter dormancy period or rather whenever the plant is not growing so much. It does usually flower during late winter/early spring(?) in the wild? I have no clue LOL

So here's an updated pic of this rare plant, photos taken 9/14/24:

Close up of the inflorescence, flowers haven't opened yet:


Flower emerges from the center of the plant. Does the mother plant that blooms die off and rely on side shoots to keep going? We shall see!





Producing tons of roots, that's a good sign of the plant being happy:



Side shoots are forming. YESSSSS!!!!

posts.body_html:
They should be flowering in early spring; perhaps something in the weather triggered an early bloom though.
From everything I could find (which was, not a lot), these are likely to be regulated in a similar way to the federally listed Sarracenia species, since it's listed as threatened/endangered. Distributing them may be similarly difficult out of state.

posts.body_html: The only transport restriction I've been able to find for this species was something about requiring written approval from the landowner before taking any from a property where they're growing wild.  I've also seen a couple mail order nurseries listing this species for sale with no restrictions listed on which states they could ship to (unfortunately both are out of stock at the moment).

posts.body_html: I think these plants are artificially rare because the few nurseries who have legitimately acquired them have not figured out how to sustainably reproduce them. That said, I expect to have near flowering to flowering sized plants ready by late winter/early 2025.

I think these plants are artificially rare because the few nurseries who have legitimately acquired them have not figured out how to sustainably reproduce them. That said, I expect to have near flowering to flowering sized plants ready by late winter/early 2025.

I suspect it also has to do with it being very niche and not a suitable selection for the average gardener which means that since there are unlikely to be a large number of gardeners buying it and of those that are interested, few will be willing to pay a high price for it, there is little incentive for nurseries to put too much effort into propagating it except as an occasional one off to keep things interesting.

This was a bit of a suprise! The plants are getting some fall colors with freezing nights and sunny, cold days! The flower stalk that was produced during the fall aborted, the flowers never opened unfortunately. Some of the other plants have an inflorescence deep in the center of the plant, so hopefully those will bloom in late winter or whenever it happens here in Northern California!
